title: Towards Efficient and Practical Multi-party Computation under Inconsistent Trust in TEEs
abstract: Secure multi-party computation (MPC) allows joint computations on sensitive data while guaranteeing privacy and correctness. In recent years, a series of MPC protocols assisted by trusted execution environments (TEEs) have been proposed to reduce overhead brought by costly cryptographic techniques. However, existing protocols either generally assume consistent trust in TEEs among all participating parties, or require dedicated designs for different applications. This prevents the protocols from being deployed in practice. To address these challenges, in this work, we propose a generic MPC protocol without assuming consistent trust in TEEs while fully utilizing heterogeneous TEEs to improve efficiency. To this end, we propose a security model to capture parties' inconsistent trust in TEEs and prove the security of our protocol under a simpler variant of the UC framework (SUC framework). In addition, we instantiate our protocol for secure aggregation based on a state-of-the-art information-theoretically secure protocol SwiftAgg+. Evaluation results among 64 parties deployed on Azure virtual machines show that our protocol reduces the running time of SwiftAgg+ by 66%. The running time of parties in our protocol is reduced by at most 91% compared to that required in SwiftAgg+.

Introduction Secure multi-party computation (MPC) allows a set of mutually distrusting parties to perform computations and guarantees the input privacy of each party and output cor- rectness. Since Yao's seminal work on garbled circuits [1], MPC has been the focus of extensive research for decades. Numerous techniques [2], [3], [4] and practical security models [5], [6], [7], [8], [9] have been proposed to advance MPC protocols for practical applications in various scenar- ios. Despite these significant improvements towards practice, MPC protocols still suffer from efficiency challenges, as communication cost typically scales with the number of participating parties and the complexity of computation tasks. For example, protocols based on secret sharing on ∗Corresponding author gate values [10], [11], [12], [13] incur round complexity linear to the depth of the circuit implementing the function, which may lead to high communication cost. In addition, the communication complexity of certain protocols [14], [15] grows superlinearly with the number of participants. These limitations hinder the deployment of MPC for complex com- putations or in settings with a large number of participants, such as privacy-preserving machine learning [16] and IoT data privacy [17], [18]. Trusted execution environments (TEEs), which isolate sensitive computations with low overhead, have been in- tegrated into several MPC protocols to enhance efficiency and security. For instance, in [19], by taking TEEs as an additional uncorrupted party, other parties send their private inputs to TEEs via secure channels established from remote attestation, and TEEs then directly perform computations on the inputs. This allows computations on the plaintexts and prevents massive communications during computation. Choudhuri et al. [20] achieve fairness of MPC protocols via TEEs and public bulletin boards, in which the output of the protocol is revealed only if TEEs confirm that the remote party will receive its output. In the literature, most prior protocols [19], [21], [20], [22] assume consistent trust in TEEs among all participating parties. However, this assumption may not hold in practice. On the one hand, TEEs are now available on different platforms, such as Intel SGX [23] and Arm OP-TEE [24]. These heterogeneous TEEs suffer from various side-channel attacks [25], which lead users to have different trust in the secrecy of TEEs across these platforms. On the other hand, even on the same platform, different parties may have different trust in the secrecy of a given TEE. Meanwhile, to fully utilize the computational efficiency of TEEs, some protocols, e.g., [21], [26], partition a function into different parts and have TEEs perform some parts of computations. To achieve this, such protocols must be care- fully designed to avoid unexpected leakage from intermedi- ate results returned by TEEs. For instance, in [26], a function is partitioned into several parts: parties' local parts computed in their hosting TEEs and an MPC part on intermediate results from TEEs. In a privacy-preserving database, to limit leakage from local database queries returned by TEEs, they 2885 DOI 10.1109/SP61157.2025.00185 introduce oblivious shuffling [27] to compute the SELECT function. However, for a complex computing task, designing such partitions to avoid privacy leakage is highly non-trivial and varies from case to case. To address the challenges mentioned above, in this paper, we first formalize MPC protocols integrated with TEEs with a security model that captures precisely the fact that participating parties may likely have inconsistent trust in the secrecy of TEEs (see Sections 2.1 and 3.3 for detailed explanations of (not) trusting TEEs in our model). This allows us to propose a generic MPC protocol, which does not rely on the assumption of consistent trust in TEEs but fully utilizes heterogeneous TEEs for improving efficiency. Under this security model, we formally prove the security of our protocol in a simpler variant of the UC framework (SUC framework) [28]. Furthermore, to demonstrate the efficiency of our protocol, we instantiate our protocol for secure aggregation based on a state-of-the-art information- theoretically secure protocol SwiftAgg+. Evaluations with 32 parties (deployed on Azure virtual machines across four global regions) report that our protocol achieves significant performance improvement compared with SwiftAgg+. In particular, when 75% of 32 parties trust TEEs on the Intel or AMD platforms, the total time of our protocol for aggre- gating inputs from all parties is 66% lower than the total time of SwiftAgg+. Technical route and design challenges. To fully utilize parties' inconsistent trust in TEEs, the main idea of our protocol is that TEEs on different platforms collect inputs from parties who trust them and then perform a software- based MPC protocol with the remaining parties. There are several challenges to implementing this idea into practice. First, we need to formalize parties' inconsistent trust in TEEs on different platforms to achieve provable security. In conventional approaches, TEEs are modeled by an ideal functionality or stateful oracles [19], [29], [30]. From the view of all parties in the protocol, the functionality or oracles behave identically. This implicitly imposes consistent trust requirements on the parties. Some recent attempts have been made to deal with this dilemma. Wu et al. [26] propose modeling hybrid trust in TEEs by an ideal functionality FT H. According to parties' different trust in TEEs, FT H decides whether to leak their inputs to adversaries. However, in reality, data leakage from TEEs is independent of the parties' trust but dependent on the security of TEEs. Their model may not fully capture scenarios in practice. Second, having TEEs run an arbitrary MPC protocol with participat- ing parties requires careful protection of communications with the programs loaded in TEEs, as corrupted hosts of TEEs may have more power than the adversaries considered by the MPC protocol. We show that previous approaches, such as the CrypTFlow compiler [31], are insecure (see Sec- tion 4.1). Finally, unlike typical scenarios where parties in an MPC protocol are fixed, under inconsistent trust in TEEs, the participating parties in the software-based MPC protocol are determined by parties' trust in TEEs. Constructing protocols in this setting and proving the security of protocols requires new methods. To summarize, our contributions are listed as follows. • We propose a generic MPC protocol integrated with TEEs. The protocol is flexible in the sense that parties' different trust in the secrecy of TEEs can be well cap- tured and, thereby, is more applicable for real scenarios. • We formalize parties' inconsistent trust and further pro- vide a formal security proof of our protocol following the real/ideal paradigm in the SUC framework. • We instantiate our protocol for secure aggregation based on SwiftAgg+. Evaluations on the global de- ployment of the protocol show that our protocol gains significantly better efficiency than SwiftAgg+. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces some necessary building blocks of our protocol. Section 3 describes the security model in detail. Section 4 provides a high-level overview and the detailed workflow of our protocol, and the security analysis of the protocol is provided in Section 5. Section 6 gives some helpful dis- cussions on how to use our protocol for different scenarios. Section 7 reports our instantiation for secure aggregation and evaluation results. Section 8 introduces some related work, and Section 9 concludes this paper. 2. Building Blocks In this section, we introduce some necessary building blocks that will be used in our protocol. 2.1. Trusted execution environments We model TEEs following the abstractions in [29], [30] by an ideal functionality Gatt, as shown in Figure 1. Parties equipped with TEEs (denoted by a set reg) can install programs prog in TEEs via install calls. Once installed, prog can be executed with given inputs inp via resume calls. The outputs of prog are signed by the private key msk of the functionality. Then, parties can verify whether or not the outputs are produced by some programs installed in Gatt using the public key mpk. The ideal functionality always honestly executes installed programs and maintains the confidentiality of their internal states. This models the integrity of program execution and the confidentiality of program data in TEEs. In recent years, side-channel attacks have been a major threat to the security of TEEs [25], [32]. Therefore, it is not appropriate to simply assume that TEEs guarantee data confidentiality, i.e., internal states of TEEs may be leaked. Instead, adversaries can corrupt TEEs through a corrupt call on Gatt. Once Gatt is corrupted, all the internal randomness of programs loaded in Gatt is exposed. In this case, our model degenerates into the transparent enclave model [30]. However, in this model, we assume adversaries cannot cause TEEs to produce incorrect outputs or steal msk to forge outputs from TEEs no matter whether TEEs are cor- rupted.
